questions.question: When are two norms $\|\cdot\|_p$ and $\|\cdot\|_q$ on $\boldsymbol{V}$ called equivalent?
options: When $a\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p\leq\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q\leq b\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for some $a,b>0$ and all $\boldsymbol{v}$.
When the norms are defined only on $\mathbb{R}$
questions.explanation: Two norms $\|\cdot\|_p$ and $\|\cdot\|_q$ on $V$ are equivalent when there exist $a,b>0$ such that $a\|v\|_p\le\|v\|_q\le b\|v\|_p$ for every $v\in V$. Each norm controls the other up to fixed constants.
questions.source_support: The definition gives the two-sided inequality with constants $a,b \gt 0$ for every vector.

option_explanations: Equality for exactly one vector is far too weak; equivalence requires the inequality for every vector $v\in V$.
The constants must be positive ($a,b>0$), and the inequality is $a\|v\|_p\le\|v\|_q$ (lower bound), not $\ge$ with negative $a$.
Norms are defined on any vector space $V$, not only on $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: If $\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_q = 2\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_p$ for every $\boldsymbol{v}$, which constants show equivalence?
questions.explanation: If $\|v\|_q=2\|v\|_p$ for every $v$, then $2\|v\|_p\le\|v\|_q=2\|v\|_p\le 2\|v\|_p$, so $a=2$ and $b=2$ prove equivalence.
questions.source_support: This directly applies the two-sided inequality in the definition.
option_explanations: $a=0$ is not allowed (must be positive); also $a=0$ would give $0\le\|v\|_q$, trivially true but not a lower bound.
$b=0$ is not allowed (must be positive); $b=0$ would force $\|v\|_q\le0$, i.e., $\|v\|_q=0$ for all $v$.
$a=-2$ is not allowed (must be positive); norms are non-negative, so a negative $a$ would be trivially satisfied but invalid.
